doc.title: Frank Alkyer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Orleans, Louisiana, January 10, 2020

chapter: Writing about jazz and reviewing records
title: Why jazz writers come from record collecting; DownBeat's detailed reviews
summary: Alkyer says jazz writers are former record collectors who loved liner notes, and describes DownBeat's reviews with star ratings, catalogue numbers and full personnel.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: What attracts DownBeat to people who write reviews on books and records?

Yeah. I think it’s, I think there are writers who like their art along the road less traveled. It’s like we are more interested in high art than pop art. And I think that they tend to be very thoughtful, very well read, very educated, very very — you know before they were jazz writers they were jazz record collectors. I don’t know of anybody who wasn’t a jazz record collector beforehand and they fell in love with the liner notes of, you know, Nat Hentoff and all the greats, you know, so those are the things that really, really, and I’m one of them. You know it’s like there’s no question I fell in love with jazz because I got to put the record on, carefully dust it off, slip the needle on, and read these liner notes from some of the greatest writers in the world, as this beautiful music is playing behind me so I can get a deeper understanding. So I think those are the things that really attract them to jazz. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

I remember that too and I’d go to the record store and you’re flipping through and sometimes it was the cover, but then you flip that thing over and sometimes you even learned about the reviewers and you learned well I like this reviewer, if he likes this record I’ll buy it.

Right. That’s exactly right, yeah. And that’s just it. You know at DownBeat we’re a little bit — we’re geeky. We just are. It’s like you look at our record reviews. There’s a star rating; there’s a review; and at the end of the review there’s a track listing with, there’s a tie; the album number, it’s like the code for the album in the catalogue; all the songs; how long this is, it’s 46 minutes, is it 53 minutes, whatever it is; a listing of all the players that are in that band. And that’s what makes our reviews different from other people. There’s no other magazine that goes to that length to really put the details out there. Because if you listen to a record by Miles Davis, Thelonious Monk, you also wanted to know, who’s the bass player? Who’s the drummer? And that goes for the people that are playing today as well.
